items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to enacting the interstate compact on educational opportunity for military children
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5805

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the education law, in relation to enacting the
interstate compact on educational opportunity for military children


 PURPOSE OF BILL :
The purpose of the compact is to remove barriers to educational
success imposed on children of military families because of the
frequent relocations and deployment of their parents by: 1)
facilitating timely enrollment to ensure that a child is not
disadvantaged due to difficulty in the transfer of education records
from the sending to the receiving school or variations in entrance or
age requirements; 2) facilitating the student placement process so
that a child is not disadvantaged by variations in attendance
requirements, scheduling, sequencing, grading, course content or
assessment; 3) facilitating qualification and eligibility for
enrollment, educational programs, and participation in extracurricular
academic, athletic, and social activities; 4) facilitating on-time
graduation; 5) providing for the promulgation and enforcement of
administrative rules implementing the provisions of this compact; 6)
providing for the uniform collection and sharing of information
between states, schools and military families; 7) promoting
coordination between this and other compact states; and 8) promoting
flexibility and cooperation between the educational system, parents,
and the student to achieve educational success for the child.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
This law creates a new article 66 in the education law of New York
State to remove barriers to educational success imposed on children of
military families (§ 3301). Highlights and changes to current
practices include:

 APPLICABILITY :
This compact applies to the children of active duty members of the
uniformed services, including members of the National Guard and
Reserve on active duty orders; members or veterans of the uniformed
services who are severely injured and medically discharged or retired
for a period of one (1) year after medical discharge or retirement;
and members of the uniformed services who die on active duty or as a
result of injuries sustained on active duty for a period of one (1)
year after death (§3303).

 RECORDS :
Unofficial or "hand-carried" education records can be utilized for
placement pending validation by official records. The last school
attended by a military child must process and furnish official
education records to the next school within ten (10) days or the time
determined under the rules by the Interstate Commission.  Military
students are allowed thirty (30) days from date of enrollment or the
time determined under the rules by the Interstate Commission to
provide immunization records or to obtain the initial immunization if
a series of immunizations are required. Military students are allowed
to continue their enrollment at the grade level they were in at their
last school (including kindergarten and first grade) regardless of age
(§ 3304).

 PLACEMENT :
When a student transfers, their next school shall honor the placement
of student in educational courses (i.e., AP, IB, vocational, honors)
pending validation by official records of their previous school. The
next school may perform subsequent evaluations.  A military student's
next school shall initially honor the placement of the student in an
educational program (i.e., gifted and talented, English as a second
language). For a military student with disabilities, their next school
shall initially provide comparable services based on his/her current
Individualized Education Program in compliance with Section 504 of the
Rehabilitation Act or Title II Plan.  The next state may perform
subsequent evaluations. The Local Education Agency (LEA) will have
flexibility in waiving course/program prerequisites. Additional
excused absences shall be granted at the discretion of the Local
Education Agency (LEA) superintendent in order to visit with his/her
active duty parent or legal guardian relative to such leave or
deployment of the parent or guardian (§3305).

 ELIGIBILITY :
A special power of attorney shall be sufficient for purposes of
enrollment and all other actions relating to eligibility.  LEAs are
prohibited from charging tuition to a transitioning student who has
been placed in the care of a non-custodial parent due to the
deployment of the custodial parent who lives in a jurisdiction other
than that of the custodial parent. State and LEAs shall facilitate
opportunities for military students to participate in extracurricular
activities regardless of application deadlines (§3306).

 GRADUATION :
LEAs shall waive specific required courses if similar course work has
been satisfactorily completed by the military student. Compact states
shall accept exit or end-of-course exams required for graduation from
the military student's previous state, national norm-referenced
achievement tests, or alternative testing in lieu of testing
requirements of their next school's state. In the event the
alternatives listed above for graduation cannot be accommodated by the
military student's last school, the last and previous LEA shall ensure
the receipt of a diploma from the previous LEA, if the student meets
the graduation requirements of the previous LEA (§3307.

 COMMISSION :
The member states will create the "Interstate Commission on
Educational Opportunity for Military Children" with the authority to
oversee the implementation of the compact. Each member state
represented at a meeting of the Interstate Commission is entitled to
one vote. The Commission will meet at least once each calendar year
(§3308 - 3318).

 JUSTIFICATION :
Military families move between postings on a regular basis. While
reassignments can often be a boon for career personnel, they usually
play havoc with the children of military families:  losing and making
new friends; adjusting to new cities and bases and changing schools.
Much remains to be done at the state and local levels to ensure that
the children of military families are afforded the same opportunities
for educational success as other children and are not penalized or
delayed in achieving their educational goals by inflexible
administrative and bureaucratic practices.

Military families place a high value on education and define the
quality of that education differently than most states or districts
that look only at issues within their boundaries. For military
families, it is not enough for children to be doing well in their
current schools - they must also be prepared for the next location.
Military families do not want special privileges for their children,
only a level playing field. Above all, they do not want their children
to make unnecessary sacrifices because of a parent's military service.
Though our military personnel have many important reasons for joining
the armed forces, it is not always easy on families. Military families
endure long separations and repeated deployments, routine moves, and
constant change.  For children and teens navigating adolescence, this
lifestyle can often be extremely difficult.  That is why it is
important for states to work together to alleviate the additional
burdens placed on military children. This legislation, enacting the
interstate compact on military children, provides the vehicle needed
to promote state cooperation.

The average military student faces transition challenges more than
twice during high school and most military children will have six to
nine different school systems in their lives from kindergarten to 12th
grade. With more than half of all military personnel supporting
families, the impacts of reassignment and long deployments are a key
consideration when making long-term life choices.

New York State is home to three active duty Army installations - Ft.
Drum, West Point, and Ft.  Hamilton. Ft. Drum houses the 10th Mountain
Division with 3 brigades (16,000+ Soldiers) and is the most deployed
Army Division in the country. In addition to the constant state of
deployment at Ft. Drum, most Soldiers and their families reside beyond
the gates in communities that can be as far as 70 miles from the
installation - away from the key military family supports.
Furthermore, there are over 15,000 geographically dispersed National
Guard and Reserve Soldiers in New York State. According to 2006 data,
it is estimated that there were more than 26,000 school age dependents
of these Soldiers.

The compact will greatly enhance the quality of life of our military
families. Designed to enable cooperation between states, the compact
allows for the uniform treatment of military children transferring
between school districts and states. It recognizes that states, no
matter how supportive they are of military children, can only control
what happens within their individual borders. By uniting with other
states in the compact, each state can ensure that "their" children
have the educational opportunities they deserve, even when those
children move to another state.

As of April 2009, thirty-six (36) states have taken some action to
adopt the Interstate Compact on Educational Opportunity for Military
Children; fifteen (15) have signed it into law, two (2) have passed it
in the legislature and delivered it to the governor for signature,
seven (7) have passed it in one house, and in twelve (12) states it
has been introduced for consideration.  Currently, an interstate
commission of education opportunity for military children is being
created for the purpose of implementing the compact. New York, with
the 10th largest population of school age dependents of military
families, needs to be at the table. In adopting this compact, the
state of New York will send a message that we, too, deem the families
of our brave Soldiers important enough to ease transition issues for
them.

Our military families help to defend our rights. The right to a free
education should not be inhibited by rules and regulations that
encumber those who should benefit most. This compact will send a
message to our heroes' children that their individual education is
important to us all.  When New York enacts this compact it will send
that message. Military families endure far more than their
counterparts and we owe them for their sacrifices.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
New bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
New York as a member of the compact will share in the expenses of the
Commission established to oversee its implementation. Currently the
total budget of the Commission is estimated to be less than $700,000.
If New York enacts this legislation and is the 16th state to do so,
its share of the Commission budget would be less than $50,000 annually
- an amount that decreases if any of the twenty-one (21) other states
currently considering the compact adopt it.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This bill will take effect immediately.

summary: Enacts the interstate compact on educational opportunity for military children, allowing children of military families to achieve educational success by facilitating smoother transfers between schools due to relocation of active duty soldiers with school-aged children in their household.
title: Enacts the interstate compact on educational opportunity for military children
